sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In this paper, we propose a Unified Law for Visual Tasks, which could be further divided into Four Laws of Computer Vision, with the goal of enabling a single framework or method to uniformly train on and perform nearly all visual tasks. Our starting point is an inspiration and hypothesis: if the world information is encoded into image, which we call World Snapshots, then image processing is world processing, and image generation is World Snapshot generation. Furthermore, if all visual and visualization tasks can be reformulated as generation tasks, then a unified method, World Snapshot Models (WSMs), can perform the vast majority of visual tasks, much as large language models have largely unified natural language processing. This paper validates these laws across more than 1,000 trained and evaluated visual tasks (defined by distinct input-output mappings) and presents a unified training framework for future visual-task research and applications.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In this paper, we propose Unified Law for Visual Tasks, which could be further divided into Four Laws of Computer Vision, with the goal of enabling single framework or method to uniformly train on and perform nearly all visual tasks. Our starting point is an inspiration and hypothesis: if the world information is encoded into image, which we call World Snapshots, then image processing is world processing, and image generation is World Snapshot generation. Furthermore, if all visual and visualization tasks can be reformulated as generation tasks, then unified method, World Snapshot Models (WSMs), can perform the vast majority of visual tasks, much as large language models have largely unified natural language processing. This paper validates these laws across more than 1,000 trained and evaluated visual tasks (defined by distinct inputoutput mappings) and presents unified training framework for future visual-task research and applications. 1. Introduction Recently, many researchers now expect computer vision to develop unified model as powerful as large language models [1, 2], often referring to such model as world model [3, 4]. This expectation is usually motivated by the hope that ideas such as predicting the next token or predicting the next state can be transferred to the visual domain [57]. However, this view faces two fundamental difficulties: visual data cannot be fully summarized by simple prompt-answer format, and computer vision tasks appear in many different forms. In this paper, we therefore attempt to formulate an ideal World Model that can move beyond these limitations and improve the unity and generality of visual methods. Insight and Hypothesis. First, we argue that what the visual domain truly needs is to encode all information into the image itself. More specifically, if all information can be encoded into the image itself, then two-dimensional image generation becomes lossless world generation.1 To verify the existence of this Unified Law, we introduce an image data format with up to 256 channels named World Snapshot Graphics (.wsg). This format stores additional information, including spatial structure, pose, physics, audio, and semantics, in extra channels. We then attempt to train model to generate images in this format, using the generation process itself as test of the proposed law. 1This statement is the Unified Law proposed in this paper. Physicists at the end of the last century referred to similar idea as the holographic principle and provided systematic arguments showing that [810], under special conditions, an (n + 1)-dimensional space can be encoded into an n-dimensional space. This also supports our view that an information-rich image can approximate world frame. Section 1 Introduction Derived Implications and Research Reframing. Furthermore, task is visual task as long as either its input or its output is visual information. Then, visual tasks can be abstracted at macro level into generation, estimation, conditional control, and reconstruction.2 These four broad categories are not arbitrary: they correspond to the four fundamental directional relations formed when RGB, text, and non-RGB world attributes serve as conditions or targets. Prior work covers each category in narrow form, such as generating only RGB or estimating few attributes from RGB; we call this narrow vision, and its extension to every world attribute broad vision. More directly, we do not want to train four separate classes of world-processing models for generation, estimation, conditional control, and reconstruction; we treat them all as forms of generation. Figure 1 presents these four task families as Lex IIV. Together, they refine and extend the Unified Law by treating all four as forms of generation, thereby avoiding having to train four broad classes of world snapshot/frame processing models. The Elephant in the Room. For concrete method, we should consider how to train unified visual generation model whose backbone can be reused by countless conditions to perform one or multiple rounds of inference. However, this immediately raises long-standing challenge: training efficiency. We should not substantially increase the number of parameters merely to make one model master more than 1,000 visual tasks; instead, we should aim for regime in which the models capabilities expand by orders of magnitude while its parameter count grows only slightly. ControlNet [11], LoRA [12], MoE [1316], IPAdapter [17], and IC-Control Style [1821] are five commonly used approaches for expanding the capabilities of existing models, but even LoRA, which can acquire new capability within several hours to several days, becomes insufficient when facing thousands of tasks. Method. We propose new method named TunnelingNet for training WSMs. Its core idea is to assign each modality to separate learning stream connected through shared generative backbone. The streams are analogous to two observers, one with typical color vision and the other with red green color blindness: each describes the same underlying object through its own representation without adopting the others visual perception. With this method, model can master thousands of visual tasks within very short time. On structured non-RGB mappings, our proposed Modality Tunneling Attention (MTA) yields 19.038.5 updatebased speedups over parameter-matched LoRA nativeattention baseline and produces the first visually identifiable Edge structure after roughly 50 updates, versus 3,8505,000 updates for the matched NJA baseline (77100 fewer updates; Fig. 5). 2These correspond to the four sub-laws. In our experiments, we find that preparing four types of interfaces can support almost all visual tasks. Section 1 Introduction Contributions. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: We propose Unified Law for Visual Tasks, which organizes all visual tasks into four broad categoriesgeneration, estimation, conditional control, and reconstructionand reformulates all four under common generative perspective, providing theoretical path toward unifying large-scale visual tasks. To support large-scale, complex visual reasoning through arbitrary, cyclic, and chained transformations among many modalities, we introduce World Snapshot Graphics (.wsg), conceptual world-frame representation and flexible image format. Its world-frame abstraction provides macro-level logic for understanding and managing modalities, while up to 256 channel IDs provide flexible operational address space for spatial, pose, physical, audio, semantic, and other world information. We introduce World Snapshot Models (WSMs), unified framework connecting the Four Laws to four generative interfaces through many-to-many correspondence. The Laws provide macro-level conceptual organization of visual tasks; the interfaces are the minimal operational basis determined by the properties of task conditions and targets and provide concrete training schemes. We propose TunnelingNet, an efficient capability-expansion method that independently trains and registers lightweight task networks inside shared frozen visual generator, enabling rapid scaling to thousands of tasks. Each generated world state can directly condition the next TunnelingNet, forming self-contained visual-processing loop across all four broad task categories and revealing an initial visual chain of thought in purely visual model. This composition opens path to large-scale, complex visual reasoning: the task space expands as modalities are added, while executable visual chains grow exponentially with chain depth. 3 1 2 3 3.1 3.2 3.3 3.4 3.5 3.6 3. 4 4.1 4.2 4.3 4.4 5 5.1 5.2 5.3 5.4 5.5 5.6 6 6.1 6.2 6.3 6.4 6.5 6.6 6.7 6.8 6.9 6.10 7 7.1 7.2 7.3 7.4 7.

This section establishes the final TunnelingNet design through controlled ablations; Section 5 measures largescale task coverage and efficiency; and Section 6 examines model outputs across the four generative interfaces. Our ablation evaluation has three primary objectives: (I) Attention Topology, determining how target and condition tokens should interact; (II) Evidence Routing and Tunnel Placement, establishing how condition/reference evidence should enter the model and which tunnels require adaptation; and (III) Rectified-Flow Objective Shaping, identifying an objective formulation that remains effective across heterogeneous output modalities. Together, these objectives determine the architecture, evidence pathways, and optimization recipe of the final TunnelingNet. To ensure that the methods selected for these three objectives are broadly effective across task types rather than specialized to single mapping, we choose four representative TunnelingNets from our broader task suite, with one task from each interface: RGB-to-Normal estimation (TunnelingNet 003), text-and-Normal-to-RGB narrow generation (TunnelingNet 270), Normal-to-Edge conditional control (TunnelingNet 275), and first-RGB-plus-Normal-to-Edge inverse rendering (TunnelingNet 313). Table 2 summarizes these four representative TunnelingNets and the final optimal configuration identified by our three-part ablation evaluation. Together, these tasks span dense geometric and photorealistic RGB outputs, sparse structural outputs, and distinct uses of current observations and first-frame visual evidence. We apply each ablation to the representative TunnelingNets for which the corresponding design choice is applicable. Agreement across interfaces supports generally effective choice, whereas consistent differences identify where interface-specific treatment is necessary. Unless stated otherwise, the FLUX.2-Klein-4B backbone, text encoder, and VAE are frozen; each TunnelingNet activates only 12.5M target-side tunnel parameters, or approximately 0.32% of the 3.9B-parameter visual backbone. We use the same data split and fixed validation set within each controlled sweep. Loss values across different target modalities are reported to establish convergence, not to rank the intrinsic difficulty of the modalities. In this ablation, NJA uses the same target-side low-rank parameterization as MTA and serves as our LoRA nativeattention baseline. MTA changes only the attention routing; the trainable parameter count, data, optimizer, batch size, and training schedule remain fixed. Native Joint Attention performs one softmax over the pooled text, target, condition, and reference keys. In controlled TunnelingNet 270 comparison at 140 updates, NJA obtained validation MSE of 0.1917, compared with 0.2155 for MTA, an 11.0% reduction. We therefore retain NJA for narrow visual generation. Figure 5(a) pairs the directly recorded validation curves with the condition, selected NJA output, and target at update 100. This result reflects the different requirements for conditioning information in RGB generation and other modality estimation tasks. Modality Tunneling Attention aims to limit the influence of the input RGB on the target generation path, allowing conditioning information to act on the target through an independent one-way channel. This mechanism is suitable for estimation, simple conditional control, and inverse-rendering tasks because it can preserve the target modalitys own generation process and prevent the input evidence from dominating. However, conditional RGB generation typically requires edges, normals, or other conditions to make larger changes to the structure and content of the reference RGB, and therefore requires fuller interaction among the condition, text, reference image, and target sequences. Native Joint Attention places these sequences in the same attention space, allowing every token to influence the entire generation sequence and thereby enabling the conditioning information to globally reorganize the RGB generation path. Therefore, Native Joint Attention is better suited to conditional RGB generation, whereas Modality Tunneling Attention is better suited to non-RGB estimation and reconstruction tasks that require the scope of the input influence to be controlled. The other three interfaces have heterogeneous, often deterministic non-RGB targets. Here, joint normalization forces target self-attention and condition attention to compete for the same probability mass. We identify this competition as the central optimization bottleneck and introduce MTA to remove it. Its native interface accepts text prompt and an optional RGB referencethe image to be editedand uses the resulting preservation prior while generating the target. The same RGB evidence can therefore enter either as native editable reference or as condition: the former encourages the backbone to preserve the supplied image, whereas the latter treats it as evidence rather than content to copy. second choice is tunnel placement: we can adapt both the condition and target lanes, or train only the target-side tunnel while leaving all evidence lanes on the frozen backbone. Routing RGB1 as native reference encourages shortcut that copies stale appearance or geometry. We instead pass its tokens through the first-frame condition branch and disable the native reference slot, so the current Normal remains the state-defining evidence. Both variants recover comparable major Edge structure, and adapting the condition side adds no visible structural gain. This does not mean that condition evidence is ignored: clean Normal and RGB1 tokens still enter the separately normalized MTA path. Rather, the result locates the task-specific learning burden at the target readout, which must translate already informative frozen evidence into the requested output modality. It is the practical counterpart of the color-vision analogy in Section 1: modality-specific streams need not acquire common internal interpretation, or learn to understand one another, to describe the same underlying state. The target tunnel learns only the translation needed by its output. Removing condition-side reinterpretation therefore reduces the optimization burden and keeps condition states adapterindependent, allowing one condition forward pass to be shared by many TunnelingNets. The panel also reveals the complementary role of visual evidence: the Normal estimate alone omits fine structures smoothed away during estimation, whereas providing RGB1 as additional evidence enables the inverse-rendering TunnelingNet to recover them. This cross-modal completion provides an empirical basis for Chain of Visual (CoV) reasoning, in which evidence retained in one visual state resolves information absent from another. With routing and tunnel placement fixed, the remaining objective-shaping choice is quantified in Table 4 and analyzed next. 4.3. Rectified-Flow Objective The initial dense-task experiments exposed two failure modes. Normal predictions retained the correct coarse shape but drifted toward low-saturation mean colors; sparse Edge predictions were progressively overwhelmed by their black background. We therefore tested task-agnostic objective changes rather than modality-specific losses. Table 4 compares plain rectified flow, single-step cleanlatent prediction, high-noise anchoring, and annealed multiresolution noise. Every model is evaluated by the same plain velocity MSE at = 1. High-noise anchoring, which assigns half of the training samples to = 0.999, is best on both representative target types and reduces their mean validation error by 42.6% relative to the baseline. Figure 8 shows that this advantage is not merely numerical. For RGB-to-Normal, plain rectified flow and multi-resolution noise recover the coarse layout but weaken the chromatic separation that encodes surface orientation; the anchored model retains more saturated, spatially coherent field. For Normal-to-Edge, the same alternatives lose much of the sparse contour support to the dominant black background, whereas anchoring preserves connected structure. Singlestep prediction is competitive in Table 4, but its decoded outputs are less consistent across these dense and sparse targets. High-noise anchoring is thus the only tested objective that improves the shared validation metric while also preserving the modality-specific information visible after decoding. We also ablated low-noise timestep shifting, Min-SNR weighting, and Huber loss. Huber produced the cleanest early visual results, and Min-SNR better resisted late degradation, but neither was consistent default. In particular, enabling all three gradually drove outputs toward the target mean: Normal kept its shape but faded, while Edge disappeared into the black background. This qualitative behavior is not captured reliably by weighted training loss, which is why we retain fixed plain-MSE validation and inspect the decoded output throughout training. The final concise recipe is therefore high-noise anchoring alone, with timestep shifting, Min-SNR, Huber, single-step prediction, and multi-resolution noise disabled. The thousand-task result therefore reflects sample-specific visual relations. What this section establishes. The same rule extends from four initial tasks to 1,148 trained tasks; the resulting routes learn the requested relation for individual examples; and target becomes substantially easier to learn when it uses representation already understood by the frozen generator. Together, these results support the Unified Law as both way of organizing visual tasks and learning principle. The law explains the large-scale success of WSM, predicts which representation of new target will be easier to acquire, and provides practical rule for building future task routes. This subsection asks three progressively harder questions. First, did the rule continue to work after the four tasks that revealed it? Second, did the resulting routes learn the requested relation for each example? Third, can we directly test the proposed reason that some representations are easier for frozen generator to acquire? The three levels move from breadth, to genuine inputoutput correspondence, to controlled test of the learning mechanism. Table 7 gives the complete logic in one place. Level I: the rule extends far beyond the tasks that revealed it. We first developed TunnelingNets 003, 270, 275, and 313, one representative task for each of the four interfaces. These four experiments established how task should be expressed and where TunnelingNet should connect to the shared generator. We then applied that rule to the other 1,144 routes. Each route was trained and evaluated while the shared generator remained frozen. The result is 1,148 trained tasks across 39 output groups. This order matters: thousands of results were obtained after the common rule had already been formed, so the rule is not summary invented separately for each finished task. The full chronological record will be provided in an expanded version. Level III: the same information is easier to learn when its representation matches the backbone. The first two levels show that the law works broadly and that the routes learn real relations. The third level tests why representation choice changes the difficulty of learning. We use RGB-tosurface-normal estimation and write every normal target in five different coordinate systems. The first is the native VAE representation seen by the generator during pretraining. The other four simply rearrange the 32 VAE channels. Each rearrangement is perfectly reversible: it removes no information and reconstructs exactly the same normal image after the inverse rearrangement. It therefore simulates modality encoded in complete but unfamiliar organization. This comparison separates two ideas that are often confused. representation can encode and decode target perfectly, while pretrained backbone may still be unfamiliar with how that representation organizes the information. Here all five versions are equally complete; only their match to the frozen generator changes. sections.content: Comparison scope. Table 8 covers five representative established design paradigms: new trainable parameter blocks (ControlNet), the MoE-style multi-expert adapter in UniControl, LoRA (DMP), expert-based MoE-family architecturesthe mixture-of-transformers in MODUS and strict sparse-MoE diffusion in Scaling Diffusion Perceptionand IC-Wrapper methods (T2I-Adapter and Uni-ControlNet). WSM introduces internal trajectory tunneling. The three blocks correspond to Interfaces : RGB-to-depth estimation, Edge-to-RGB generation, and any-to-any control. We also include VGGT as taskInterface evaluates transfers specific depth estimator. among edge, relative depth, surface normal, and humanpart segmentation signals. Both WSM and MODUS support broader transfer inventory; we select these tasks as representative cross-section of structured understanding, spanning object and region boundaries, scene-scale spatial organization, local surface orientation, and human semantics. Across all three externally comparable interfaces and all five representative tasks, WSM leads every reported quality metric, demonstrating that its advantage holds across all five adaptation paradigms. Interface combines first-frame RGB evidence with later auxiliary observation, for which we found no released image-level method with matching inputs. Most remaining mappings enabled by this interface similarly define new task settings without like-for-like external comparator. Evaluation data. Images from widely used benchmark datasets may have been included in the web-scale pretraining corpora of large foundation models. We therefore use the AVIS evaluation set, which is less commonly used for dense prediction, and generate the task annotations evaluated here ourselves. This choice reduces the likelihood of direct overlap with existing imageannotation pairs. None of the evaluation images or annotations is used to train WSM. semantic analysis of the scene captions also finds almost no close match between the evaluation scenes and the WSM training descriptions. Every method receives the same AVIS inputs and targets. The external methods use their released checkpoints, and WSM uses its trained TunnelingNets without further optimization. The WSM TunnelingNets for depth and Edge-to-RGB use TunnelingNets 1 and 424; TunnelingNet 424 uses its recommended nativereference route. Interface uses TunnelingNets 275, 119, and 434 for Normal-to-Edge, Relative-Depth-to-Normal, and Edge-to-Human-Segmentation, respectively. The comparison therefore measures all methods on the same unseen scenes and annotations. Section 5 Large-Scale Quantitative Evaluation 5.4 External Comparison on the AVIS Evaluation Set Interface metrics. For NormalEdge, accuracy, falsepositive rate (FPR), and specificity are computed from shared binary edge threshold. Surface normals are decoded into the same physical XYZ convention and evaluated only over valid, unpadded pixels. Mean and median errors are measured in degrees, and the three threshold accuracies report the fraction of pixels below 11.25, 22.5, and 30. For EdgeHuman Segmentation, WSM predicts the complete channel-103 target with background and five humanpart labels. MODUS produces category-conditioned person mask, so the shared comparison merges the five humanpart labels into one human foreground class for both WSM and the target. We report pixel accuracy, mean IoU (mIoU), human-foreground IoU, mean class accuracy (mAcc), and macro-F1 under this common ontology. Task parameters and training efficiency. Each WSM task adds 12.5M-parameter TunnelingNet to the shared 4B model, only 0.31% of the base model. Training Sample Budget measures optimizer updates times global batch size. Across the eleven methodtask comparisons with recoverable budgets, external methods process 230145.5K times as many training examples as WSM; ratios for packedsequence models remain lower bounds. WSM is 29.4K times more sample-efficient than the evaluated external methods on average and 2.53K times more sampleefficient at the median, while leading every reported quality metric. The reported training costs show the same scale of advantage. The Edge-to-RGB TunnelingNet reaches its selected checkpoint in 8.5 minutes on one A100. ControlNet Canny 1.1 alone continues training on eight A100s for three days, with more than 1,176 A100-hours across its complete training path, while UniControl reports more than 5,000 A100-hours. The three any-to-any TunnelingNets reach their selected checkpoints in 9.39.6 hours on one A100, compared with 5,664 GH200-hours for MODUS; the depth TunnelingNet takes 11.0 A100-hours, compared with 13.8K A100-hours for VGGT. WSM reaches its strongest checkpoints in minutes to hours on one GPU, while several evaluated external methods report thousands of accelerator-hours. Across the 15 external methodtask comparisons, WSM is 11.02 times faster than the evaluated external methods on average and 1.89 times faster at the median. Its MAE/RMSE are 0.130/0.162, compared with the next-best 0.167/0.216 from MODUS. WSM also surpasses VGGT, the CVPR 2025 Best Paper Award recipient, which obtains 0.243/0.296, and Marigold, CVPR 2024 Best Paper Award Candidate, which obtains 0.247/0.291. Scaling Diffusion Perception, strict sparseMoE DiT with eight experts and top-2 routing, obtains 0.232/0.274. WSM reaches Pearson/Spearman correlations of 0.935/0.907 and leads all three threshold accuracies. WSM predicts the normalized depth target directly; external outputs receive the fixed percentile-based linear mapping, with depth direction aligned before scoring. For conditional RGB, WSM leads all five quality measures against all five external methods. Against ControlNet, the ICCV 2023 Best Paper Award recipient, WSM reduces MAE from 0.276 to 0.087 and MSE from 0.120 to 0.021, while increasing PSNR from 9.90 to 19.51 and SSIM from 0.127 to 0.762. Evaluation with Independent Public Annotations Purpose and task setting. Sections 5.4 and 5.5 compare WSM with prior methods through the three interfaces for which released, input-matched baselines are available. The post-release experiment additionally makes the evaluated images unavailable during model training. Its geometric annotations, however, still follow the WSG data-preparation convention used to train WSM. This leaves separate question: does WSM remain competitive when the desired outputs are defined by unrelated public annotators? This distinction is important because new images test visual transfer, whereas new annotation conventions also test whether method has learned the task itself. We therefore combine both changes: every evaluated image postdates the training of all compared models, and every geometric condition and target is defined by public annotator outside the WSG preparation pipeline. Success in this setting requires the learned interface to survive changes in scene content, numeric convention, and annotation family at the same time. Table 10 answers this question on five representative tasks across the three reported interfaces. Interface uses RGBRelative Depth to test scene-scale spatial estimation. Interface uses EdgeRGB to test whether method can synthesize appearance while respecting an explicit structural condition. Interface covers three target types: surface normals, human foreground segmentation, and edges. Relative DepthNormal tests surface recovery from scene-scale ordering; NormalHuman Segmentation tests semantic transfer; and NormalEdge tests boundary reconstruction from local orientation. Each direction uses identical inputoutput definitions for WSM and the released MODUS model. Interface is not included because, as discussed in Section 5.4, no released image-level method accepts its matched combination of observations. Replacing annotations while keeping the evaluation fixed. We retain the post-release scene pool, image crops, trained models, training-cost calculation, and official inference procedures. We replace the geometric annotation pipeline: OpenCV Canny [47] produces binary edges, Depth Anything V2 Large [63] produces relative depth, Marigold Normals v1.1 [55] produces camera-space surface normals, and Mask2Former-Swin-Large trained on ADE20K [64] produces human foreground masks. Every method receives the same independently generated conditions and targets. Relative-depth maps receive fixed perimage 2nd98th-percentile linear map to [0, 1], and normal metrics operate directly on physical unit vectors. WSG serves only as the storage and input-encoding format for WSM; it does not generate any annotation used in this experiment. No method is retrained, calibrated, or adapted 36 Section 5 Large-Scale Quantitative Evaluation 5.6 Evaluation with Independent Public Annotations to these annotations. The comparison therefore isolates transfer to an independent task definition while keeping the evaluated images, crops, checkpoints, and methodspecific inference procedures fixed. Qualitative comparison. Figures 18 and 19 expose the predictions behind Table 10. Under the independent depth target, WSM preserves continuous scene ordering and prominent object boundaries across indoor, outdoor, and object-centric scenes. The conditional RGB panel reproduces the Canny-controlled comparison from Figure 16, since this condition was already independent of WSG. In Interface , WSM produces coherent surface-normal fields from independently estimated relative depth, clean human foreground mask from surface normals, and structured edges from the same normal representation. These three transfers cover geometric surfaces, human semantics, and boundaries. The visual comparisons confirm that WSMs advantage remains visible when both structured inputs and evaluation targets are supplied by independent public annotators. Overall performance. WSM leads every reported quality column in the three Interface task blocks. Together with the RGB-generation comparison, these results cover appearance, surface geometry, human semantics, and boundary structure under independent annotation conventions. The advantage is therefore not tied to single target space or one favorable metric; it persists across the three distinct any-to-any targets shown in Table 10. The same result is obtained with only 12.5M trainable target-side parameters per TunnelingNet and 4402,000 single-sample updates. All checkpoints and accounting rules remain unchanged, so the trainingand inferenceefficiency advantages in Section 5.5 transfer directly to the independent annotations. WSM consequently delivers the strongest overall quality across every externally comparable interface while preserving its orders-of-magnitude task-acquisition advantage. Estimation and reconstruction. For RGBRelative Depth, WSM obtains the best boundary precision at both twoand three-pixel tolerances (0.815/0.848). Its boundary false-positive rate, gradient MAE, and gradient RMSE are all second-best, trailing SenseNova only narrowly. WSM surpasses VGGT, the CVPR 2025 Best Paper Award recipient, on all five reported depth measures. Relative to VGGT, WSM raises boundary precision by 53.5% at two pixels and 40.4% at three pixels, while reducing boundary false positives by 39.9%, gradient MAE by 28.4%, and gradient RMSE by 13.4%. It reaches this result with 1,740 singlesample updates on one A100; the reported comparison systems use sample budgets ranging from 229.9 to at least Section 5 Large-Scale Quantitative Evaluation 5.6 Evaluation with Independent Public Annotations sparse MoE; and VGGT uses discriminative feed-forward regression. WSM is not specialized to any one of their output domains. The same frozen backbone and the same tunneling principle outperform these alternatives across depth, conditional RGB, and condition-to-condition surface prediction. The award-winning comparisons make this breadth especially concrete: WSM exceeds the CVPR 2025 Best Paper Award recipient VGGT on all five displayed depth measures, and it exceeds the ICCV 2023 Best Paper Award recipient ControlNet on all seven conditional-generation measures. It also outperforms the reference-enabled IPAdapterControlNet combination on those seven measures. The result is therefore cross-paradigm improvement, not an isolated gain over one architecture family. Conclusion. The three evaluations isolate complementary concerns. Section 5.4 compares representative methods on common held-out set; Section 5.5 removes possible image-level pretraining overlap; and this section replaces the WSG annotation convention with public annotators. In this final setting, WSM remains strongest in conditional RGB generation and every structured transfer, while retaining the best depth-boundary precision. Across the five tasks, it outperforms award-winning specialized systems, modern diffusion perception models, referenceconditioned adapters, and 14B MoE model, while adapting only 12.5M-parameter TunnelingNet for each task. The 23 first-place and three second-place results show that WSMs advantage persists across new visual content, independent target definitions, three interfaces, five representative tasks, and fundamentally different modeling paradigms. This directly demonstrates that TunnelingNet can make far more effective and powerful use of frozen generative backbone through extremely lightweight training, thereby adding strong new capabilities at scale. This represents an advance over the prior paradigm-level approaches evaluated here. 2.94K times larger where accounting is available. WSM therefore combines the strongest measured boundary preservation with exceptionally rapid acquisition, even when the target-depth convention is defined by an unrelated public estimator. Conditional RGB generation. The EdgeRGB condition is generated by OpenCV Canny for every method. WSM leads all seven reported quality measures, covering edge consistency, pixel error, PSNR, and SSIM. Its advantage over ControlNet, the ICCV 2023 Best Paper Award recipient, therefore holds under standard public edge convention rather than WSG-derived target. The advantage also holds against the reference-enabled combination of IP-Adapter and ControlNet: WSM reduces MAE by 66.1% and MSE by 83.5%, raises PSNR from 11.47 to 19.83, and raises SSIM from 0.226 to 0.845. These gains are learned in 440 updates8.5 minutes on one A100 with training-sample budget at least 11.6K times smaller than every baseline for which complete budget is recoverable. This is complete quality sweep achieved by minute-scale TunnelingNet, including against both Best Paper control architecture and its reference-image extension.

Conversely, when target depends on boundaries or appearance not determined by structured condition alone, RGB-assisted inverse rendering restores scene-specific cues from the observation. Omitting RGB yields geometrysupported abstraction; supplying RGB restores observationspecific detail. We next examine every remaining qualitative figure in order, separating spatial fidelity, value calibration, and categorical assignment. 6.5. RGB Estimation Geometry and motion. Figure 21 shows that the same RGB condition can be translated into six geometrically distinct representations. Normals, curvature, and absolute depth are especially stable (QS 0.959, 0.896, and 0.936). Relative depth and the direction-consistent flow example retain the dominant scene layout (0.850 and 0.968), while Edge is less uniform (0.837) because thin boundaries are only weakly determined by local appearance. The contrast is consistent with human geometric reasoningsurface orientation can remain clear even when an exact metric distance or boundary convention is ambiguous. Articulated structure. Figure 22 tests DWPose, SMPLX, MediaPipe Pose, XPose, MediaPipe Seg, and Universal Pose rather than six renderings of one dense field. Their common success is structural: joints remain connected in recognizable body layout. In the third row, the prediction occasionally completes joints that are missing or malformed in the automatically produced MediaPipe pseudo ground truth. This does not make the proxy annotation infallible; instead, it shows that the learned human prior can denoise imperfect supervision. The fourth-row XPose targets are likewise produced by an automatic detector rather than manual annotation, and their quality remains limitation of the present dataset. Nevertheless, their scale supplies enough weak supervision for the TunnelingNet to recover characteristic skeletal structure. The result is evidence that the proposed paradigm can discover useful structure from large, imperfectly annotated corpora, while also identifying where better labels would improve the model. The MediaPipe Seg row complements these skeletal encodings with dense estimate of human support. Its official sixregion palette distinguishes background, hair, body skin, Section 6 Qualitative Evaluation 6.4 Interface Comparison face skin, clothes, and accessories. We render the TunnelingNets generated field through this discrete palette before categorical-refiner correction, so the figure exposes both region support and direct class assignment. The final row extends the same image-to-structure formulation beyond fixed human representations: custom TunnelingNet recovers the category-independent red-joint, white-link Universal Pose used by MP-100 from an RGB observation. Physical properties. Figure 23 contains seven objectaligned fields whose QS values lie between 0.974 and 1.000. Solid and surface volume, weight, support, friction, and density preserve nearly the same object support while changing the value carried inside it. This result should not be read as direct measurement of an objects physical constants; rather, it shows that the TunnelingNet learns the datasets encoded physical estimate without losing spatial correspondence to the observed object. Material and PBR appearance I. Figure 24 compares ambient and diffuse color, opacity, specular color, shininess, base color, and diffuse response. The strong opacity, specular-color, shininess, and base-color examples show that broad, piecewise-smooth appearance attributes can be transported with little spatial drift. Ambient and diffuse color remain more sensitive to illumination, making them less directly recoverable than support or intrinsic appearance. Material and PBR appearance II. Figure 25 exposes the harder part of the PBR interface. Height, metallicity, and specular response remain strong, whereas roughness and opacity maps deviate more visibly from the target. These channels require calibrated local intensity rather than only correct object mask; consequently, prediction may retain the right region while assigning an imperfect material value. Segmentation and semantics. Figure 26 demonstrates that continuous Alpha and categorical masks can share the same generative interface. The selected material, entity, object, container, and semantic examples have high mIoU and dominant-class accuracy, so both the generated support and principal palette label are correct in these cases. They are deliberately readable successful examples, not substitute for the aggregate matrices: Figure 45 later presents the final outputs of the complete categorical TunnelingNets. 6.6. Narrow RGB Generation Geometric control. Figure 27 reverses the RGBestimation direction. Depth, normals, curvature, edges, and flow now constrain RGB synthesis while text and optional historical RGB provide appearance. The six examples range from QS 0.898 to 0.979; curvature and normal control are particularly stable, while flow is weakest. This ordering reflects how directly condition fixes the target frame: static geometry constrains most pixels, whereas flow must be interpreted jointly with temporal and appearance context. Human control. Figure 28 replaces dense geometry with articulated human representations. DWPose, SMPL-X, MediaPipe Pose/Class, and XPose all produce coherent RGB frames, with QS spanning 0.8090.947. The lower SMPLX and XPose scores expose the difficulty of reconstructing texture and background from sparse pose evidence. QS measures target-frame reconstruction and therefore complements, rather than replaces, visual inspection of whether the requested pose actually redirects the person. Object-level physical control. Figure 29 covers object category, volume, weight, support, and friction conditions. Despite their low visual bandwidth, these fields yield recognizable frames because the physical and category channels narrow the set of compatible appearances. Class and material control. Figure 30 continues with material class, density, friction coefficient, container, entity category, and ambient color. These conditions remain useful even when their nonzero information occupies only small part of the canvas. Text and historical RGB remain necessary because the structured channel determines what must be preserved but does not fully specify photometric appearance. Appearance control. Figure 31 separates direct color fields from derived PBR controls. Base color and diffuse response retain broad object support, while height, roughness, and metallicity constrain appearance more indirectly. The comparison shows how text and historical RGB resolve the many RGB images compatible with low-bandwidth material field. PBR and semantic control. Figure 32 completes the readable source sweep with specular response, opacity map, and semantic masks. The PBR fields preserve continuous appearance structure; semantic mask constrains identity and support but intentionally leaves within-class texture and illumination underdetermined. 6.7. Conditional Control Geometry-to-geometry transport. Figure 33 spans QS 0.7340.967, revealing that geometric channels are not interchangeable merely because they share image coordinates. Relative-depth-to-Normal and Flow-to-Normal are strong, whereas Normal-to-Edge is lower because smooth 66 Section 6 Qualitative Evaluation 6.7 Conditional Control normals suppress texture boundaries present in the target edge convention. The cleaner predicted edge is thus meaningful geometric abstraction, even when it does not minimize every target pixel error. Geometry and pose. Figure 34 crosses dense surfaces with sparse body structure. Edge-to-DWPose and DWPoseto-Normal reach 0.975 and 0.939, showing that visible boundaries can localize body and skeleton can guide coarse surface orientation. Curve-to-SMPL-X and MediaPipe-to-Curvature reach 0.907 and 0.663, as they require recovering quantities absent from the source rather than translating shared structure. Pose-system conversion. Figure 35 isolates six directed conversions among DWPose, SMPL-X, and MediaPipe Pose. All six retain strong joint organization, while DWPose-to-SMPL-X is the hardest at 0.810. The asymmetry is important: two pose systems can describe the same person yet expose different joints, surface priors, and occlusion conventions, so reversing an edge is not the same learning problem. Physical-property transport. Figure 36 is close to ceiling for volume, weight, support, density, and friction mappings (0.9430.998). These tasks share object-aligned support and often vary mainly in the value assigned inside that support. The result explains the coherent high-score block in the quantitative matrix without implying that arbitrary physical variables are causally equivalent. Cross-family transport. Figure 37 tests deliberately less homogeneous pairs. Opacity-to-SolidVolume and DiffuseColor-to-Density remain strong, while Density-toAmbient is harder. Spatial support transfers readily across families, but an appearance value cannot always be inferred from physical scalar. The two categorical rows additionally test whether shared support can carry discrete label rather than only continuous value. PBR transport. Figure 38 isolates four PBR conversions. Base-color and diffuse relations remain strongly constrained by shared material support. The fourth row, roughness-to-metallic, exposes fundamentally weaker form of evidence: roughness does not determine metallicity, so the TunnelingNet can only exploit learned visual regularitiesfor example, that metallic surfaces are often smoothto form plausible estimate. This is not deterministic recovery, and the resulting degradation is expected. Nevertheless, the prediction goes beyond copying aligned pixels: it reveals cross-attribute visual association that can be strengthened as supervision and coverage improve. Categorical Output Analysis For categorical targets, the categorical refiner is an integral component of the corresponding TunnelingNet and is enabled by default during inference. This gives sparse annotations and newly digitized structures the same operational status as an existing image-like endpoint without renumbering the released dense graph or retraining the shared generator. Universal Pose is the first explicit example of this extension path. We render the category-independent MP-100 landmark annotations as sparse red joints and white links on black canvas, register RGB and Universal Pose as named nodes in custom task graph, and train one additional TunnelingNet. The final row of Figure 22 is 10-step generation result on the evaluation set from that TunnelingNet. It extends the fixed human-pose representations above it to the articulated structure of animals and objects while preserving the same conditionpredictiontarget interface. Subsequent additions can be reported in this subsection with their data source, task definition, selected model, metrics, and qualitative artifact. Visible appearance resolves body extent and occlusion, but single RGB frame still cannot uniquely determine every differential surface quantity. Pose inversion. Figure 41 provides the cleanest evidence that the reference image complements, rather than replaces, the structured condition. Compared directly with the condition-only conversions in Figure 35, the RGB-assisted results are visibly more complete and stable: the observation resolves person count, visible body extent, and occlusion cues that sparse pose representation leaves ambiguous. Three of the six directed conversions improve quantitatively; DWPose-to-SMPL-X rises from 0.810 to 0.816 and SMPL-X-to-MediaPipe from 0.914 to 0.925. The pose channel specifies the requested representation, while RGB restores the scene evidence needed to instantiate it accurately. Physical inversion. Figure 42 retains the near-ceiling behavior of the physical block, now with RGB evidence. All four displayed mappings remain between 0.938 and 0.999 QS. Differences are small because object support was already available in the structured condition; RGB mainly sharpens visible boundaries. Cross-family inversion. Figure 43 shows where observation is most useful. Density-to-Ambient improves substantially, while opacity-, diffuse-, and solid-volumeconditioned mappings remain stable. The categorical rows show the same principle for discrete targets: RGB can clarify visible object identity, but cannot repair missing spatial support region. The evidence supports selective assistance rather than claim that RGB universally dominates structured transport. PBR inversion. Figure 44 isolates four RGB-assisted PBR conversions. Our ablation study shows how TunnelingNet acquires new visual route. We find that attention topology, evidence routing, tunnel placement, and high-noise trajectory supervision all shape how quickly task-specific TunnelingNet learns its target representation while preserving the RGB prior. The resulting configuration produces recognizable structure within tens of updates and reaches up to approximately 100 greater training efficiency than the parametermatched native-attention baseline. Our quantitative study then asks how widely this recipe holds: it evaluates 1,148 visual tasks, with one independently deployable TunnelingNet per task, across 39 output groups, four interfaces, and 18,191 end-to-end inference evaluations. Our qualitative study lets us inspect the visual relationships behind those numbers across geometry, articulated humans, motion, physical properties, materials, PBR appearance, segmentation, categorical identity, and RGB synthesis. Together, our experiments give consistent picture: shared generator can learn wide vocabulary of World Snapshot transformations when each route receives focused parameters and clearly routed evidence. Scale and strength of our baseline. We summarize continuous outputs with the higher-is-better quality score QS and categorical outputs with dominant-class accuracy (DAcc), abbreviated together as QS/DAcc. Across the 1,147 tasks with valid primary score, 779 (67.9%) exceed QS/DAcc = 0.8. Within the 969 continuous tasks, 744 (76.8%) exceed QS = 0.8, 537 (55.4%) exceed QS = 0.9, and the mean QS is 0.860. These measurements give us confidence that the strong region extends across hundreds of heterogeneous mappings. The paired matrices also show natural dependence on the visual evidence shared by the condition and target. 7.2. Unified Task Graph and Model Scale Why the directed graph matters. Each WSM task is directed path from available evidence to World Snapshot target. Moving variable from the condition side to the target side asks the model to generate that variable. RGB therefore becomes one node in much larger generative domain that also includes geometry, pose, motion, material, 68 Section 7 Discussion physics, semantics, and audio. This construction makes training naturally parallel: every edge shares the frozen backbone, while its small tunnel can be scheduled, optimized, and validated independently. It also makes capabilities compositional. generated variable can become evidence for the next edge, so longer visual chains can be assembled from learned paths. The complete modular WSM comprises one shared backbone, resident collection of trained TunnelingNets and an explicit task router. Independent TunnelingNet optimization and physical sharding of the TunnelingNet files enable parallel training and modular distribution without changing this model boundary. All TunnelingNets remain registered together, while task key sparsely activates one edge and visual chain activates selected sequence. This resident-versus-active organization is analogous to sparsely activated expert models. WSM routes with an explicit visual-task key; conventional expert models commonly learn their gating. We verified that each of the 1,148 frozen dense TunnelingNets contains exactly 12,510,208 tunnel parameters, giving 14.362B TunnelingNet parameters in total. Together with the 3.9B visual backbone and 0.282B parameters from the 180 deployed categorical refiners, the complete resident visual parameter bank is approximately 18.54B parameters. In this complete deployment form, WSM v1 Augustus is an 18B-class model with 1,148 selectable visual tasks.6 single inference route activates one 12.51M tunnel, so its active visual parameter count remains approximately 3.913B; categorical routes add only 1.541.60M active refiner parameters. Replicating the 3.9B backbone once for every evaluated task would already require approximately 4.48T visual parameters. Sharing one backbone therefore reduces this task-library parameterization by about 241, while retaining dedicated generative route for every task. 7.3. Most computer-vision models are built around one task, and broadly capable systems usually collect small set of taskspecific interfaces. WSM v1 places 1,148 evaluated tasks inside one generative system, while its released dense task graph configures 3,042 possible mappings. Relative to the conventional scope of one to ten tasks, this expands the task count by roughly two to three orders of magnitude. It also changes the unit of progress: we can grow one directed generative graph by adding World Snapshot variables and routes, and every new route becomes part of the same model. In our controlled wall-clock records for Tasks 003, 275, and 313, native attention required 12h56m32s, 13h08m09s, and 15h29m53s, whereas TunnelingNet required 46m55s, 47m01s, and 27m18s at the selected milestones. This wall-clock result complements the 19.038.5 update-count acceleration and the 77100 earlier emergence of recognizable structure in Sec. 4. 7.4. Unifying and Expanding Computer Vision This section tests the central scope claim of the Unified Law. We ask two questions. First, can the established tasks of computer vision be expressed within the WSM interface system? Second, after those established tasks are removed, how many tasks evaluated by WSM define genuinely new visual problems? The first question measures unification; the second measures expansion. We use Papers with Code as the historical reference because it maintained one of the broadest public catalogs of computer-vision research, connecting named tasks with papers, datasets, code, and benchmarks. Its final public records contain 1,477 visual or vision-related tasks, which we use as representative inventory of the established field [65]. For unification, we examine whether each historical task can be written as route through the WSM interfaces. For expansion, we compare the 1,148 tasks evaluated by WSM v1 with this inventory and count the evaluated tasks that have no historical counterpart. The complete matching rules and task-level records are detailed in an expanded version. The result is direct. All 1,477 historical visual tasks can be expressed within the WSM interfaces, giving 100% compatibility with the representative historical inventory. After historical overlaps are removed, 6551,056 of the 1,148 evaluated WSM tasks are new. Relative to the 1,477 established visual tasks, WSM therefore expands the computervision task space by 44.371.5%. Figure 47 presents these two results. Together, these findings establish both parts of the claim. WSM provides one generative interface system for the established field of computer vision, and it substantially enlarges that field with executable task definitions and trained baselines. Its dense graph already contains 3,042 mappings, and each newly aligned modality creates further families of estimation, generation, control, and reconstruction tasks. We call this direction Task-Generative Computer Vision: visual framework that unifies the existing task space and 70 Section 7 Discussion 7.4 Unifying and Expanding Computer Vision systematically creates new tasks beyond it. Position and interpretation of evidence. WSM makes three complementary claims, each supported at its appropriate experimental scale. First, WSG and the four interfaces provide one operational rule for expressing heterogeneous visual computations as directed generation. Second, WSM v1 turns that rule into an executable system: 1,148 distinct inputoutput tasks have their own trained TunnelingNets and end-to-end inference results within one shared-backbone model. Here, unified refers to the shared representation, generative backbone, route-acquisition rule and router. Independently optimized TunnelingNets remain sparsely activated components within that model, not replications of the full backbone. Third, the historical analysis shows that the four interfaces cover 1,477 historical visual tasks, while the 1,148 figure separately measures tasks that were actually trained and evaluated. Keeping these quantities distinct makes the breadth claim directly auditable. The validation scale was deliberately increased from tens of representative routes, to hundreds of cross-family mappings, and finally to 1,148 frozen tasks. Prior generalist vision systems commonly remain at tens of tasks, and reports beyond one hundred are rare. WSM therefore moves the empirical frontier to 1,148 separately trained and evaluated tasks: more than an order of magnitude beyond even 100-task system, 2938 beyond 3040-task system, and two to three orders beyond the conventional one-toten task setting. These levels answer different questions: matched MTANJA ablations isolate TunnelingNet acquisition behavior; QS/DAcc and 18,191 generated outputs measure system-wide coverage; task-native metrics establish target-specific quality; and AVIS, post-release imagery, and independent public annotations establish transfer after acquisition. In this last setting, zero-shot and training-free mean that route is trained once and then applied to unseen datasets and annotation conventions without datasetspecific retraining. Likewise, the reported budget ratios measure marginal task acquisition after the respective pretrained priors, whereas the matched attention ablations isolate the contribution of TunnelingNet itself. This layered protocol evaluates scale without equating coverage with identical ceiling accuracy: the complete score distributions and disclosed failure regions identify which TunnelingNets merit further improvement while preserving the systemlevel evidence that one method can acquire, register, and execute more than one thousand visual tasks. Finally, the breadth and chain equations describe the tasks available in the graph. An inputoutput mapping is distinct task because changing either its available evidence or its target changes the learned conditional distribution; opposite directions are therefore different visual problems. sections.content: Why law, and why vision now? Empirical laws in artificial intelligence capture reproducible regularities over defined regimes. The canonical study Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models [66] examines cross-entropy under one autoregressive language-modeling objective: the models are trained on WebText2, and the analysis establishes predictive power laws over model size, dataset size, and compute, with trends spanning six to eight orders of magnitude. Its importance does not come from separately validating every NLP task, but from discovering stable empirical relation that compresses observations and predicts behavior outside individual runs. In task diversity, that evidence centers on one learning objective; WSM instead realizes one visual organizing principle through 1,148 separately trained visual tasks, 39 output groups, four interfaces, and 18,191 generated outputs. On count of learning objectives, one is less than 0.1% of 1,148. The two laws are validated along different scientific axes: scaling law is tested by depth along model, data, and compute scales, whereas unifying law is tested by breadth across heterogeneous visual tasks. The breadth of 1,148 tasks directly supports the unification claim. The broader scientific precedent is clear: an empirical law in AI is established by reproducible regularity over defined regime. The law and its empirical realization. The Unified Law has two deliberately separated levels. The law itself is representation statement: once the information required by visual task can cross the model boundary without losing task-relevant distinction, the task can be written as conditional generation of requested world fields from known world fields. WSM and TunnelingNet provide an empirical realization of this statement: shared generator can acquire many such directed relations through small, independently installed routes. The first level does not depend on particular parameterization; the measured parameter counts and training times belong to the second. The second asks whether these routes follow each individual input; deliberately pairing their fixed predictions with the wrong targets increases error in every interface. The third asks why representation choice changes learning difficulty. We write the same surface-normal target in five lossless coordinate systems. Conclusion We presented the Unified Law for Visual Tasks, which expresses visual tasks as transformations among image-like World Snapshots. World Snapshot Graphics encodes RGB and auxiliary attributes in representation with up to 256 channels, while four interfaces express generation, estimation, conditional control, and reconstruction in one generative formulation. Together, these interfaces and TunnelingNet realize 1,148 evaluated visual tasks within dense graph of 3,042 configured mappings. We validate both the method and the Unified Law at this scale, establishing their effectiveness across more than one thousand tasks. Our experiments show that TunnelingNet preserves the pretrained RGB-synthesis prior while efficiently acquiring structured visual transformations, reaching up to approximately 100 greater training efficiency than the parametermatched native-attention baseline. Across all evaluated tasks, WSM also achieves consistently strong performance, surpassing specialized prior methodsincluding Best Paper and Best Paper Candidate systemson the reported metrics. The mathematical scalability of the Unified Law further connects model growth to task growth: aligned modalities expand direct-task breadth quadratically, visual chains expand compositional depth exponentially, and independent task routes can be trained in parallel. These routes are registered parameters of one modular WSM and are sparsely activated by an explicit task key; independent optimization and physical sharding do not make them standalone models. WSM therefore provides one extensible generative foundation for large and continually growing vocabulary of visual tasks. Its longer-term trajectory is to unify, expand, and ultimately transcend the fixed task boundaries of conventional Computer Vision. In addition, we compare WSM with the visual tasks established before this work and obtain two findings. First, among the tasks recorded by Papers with Code, 1,477 are visual or vision-related tasks, broadly representing the vast established field of Computer Vision. All 1,477 tasks are compatible with the WSM interfaces and can be expressed by the same system. After half century of development, we bring the vast field of Computer Vision into unified generative framework. Second, WSM creates 6551,056 entirely new visual tasks and expands Computer Vision by 44.371.5%. Every evaluated task is accompanied by trained baseline. Together, these results establish WSM as task-generative foundation that consolidates the historical field and opens substantially larger visual-task space.
